title: Time management section by section
lines: The new TOEFL is short, but it is fast. Many test takers know enough English to score well and still lose points because they spend too long on a few items and then rush the rest. This article gives you a time plan for each section and simple habits to keep it.
## The big picture
- Reading: 50 items in about 30 minutes, an average of well under a minute per item.
- Listening: 47 items in about 29 minutes, but much of that time is spent listening. You answer after each recording, so the pace is partly set for you.
- Writing: 12 items in 23 minutes, with most of the time going to the two writing tasks.
- Speaking: 11 items in 8 minutes. The timing is fully controlled by the test; your job is to use it well.
! Always follow the on-screen timer. Your sense of time changes under stress.
## Reading

Different item types take different amounts of time. Complete the Words items are quick once you have read the paragraph; Read in Daily Life questions are moderate; academic passage questions take the longest.
- Complete the Words: read the whole paragraph quickly first for meaning, then fill the gaps. Do not stop for long on a single word; come back to it if the module lets you.
- Read in Daily Life: read the questions first, then scan the text for each answer. These texts are short and practical.
- Academic Passage: skim the passage for the main idea (about 30-45 seconds), then answer the questions, going back to the relevant sentence for each one.
- Set a checkpoint: at about half the module time, you should be roughly halfway through the items. If you are behind, speed up on the next easy items.
- Never leave a blank. If time is almost over, choose an answer for every remaining item.
## Listening
- You hear each recording once. Before it starts, read anything on screen that tells you the context (who is talking, what kind of talk it is).
- Answer each question promptly. Long hesitation does not improve your memory of the recording.
- If you do not know an answer, eliminate options that contradict your notes or were not mentioned, choose, and move on. The next recording needs your full attention.
## Writing
A practical split for 23 minutes:

- Build a Sentence (10 items): work quickly and keep moving. Find the start of the sentence (often the subject or the question word), then the verb, then the rest. Check the full sentence reads naturally before you go on.
- Write an Email (7 minutes): about 1 minute to read and plan, 5 minutes to write, 1 minute to check.
- Academic Discussion (10 minutes): about 1-2 minutes to read and choose a position, 7 minutes to write, 1 minute to check.
! Save one minute at the end of each writing task to check. Fixing a wrong verb form or a missing article is quick and visible to the scorer.
## Speaking
- Listen and Repeat: focus completely during the sentence. Start speaking as soon as you are allowed, while the sentence is still fresh. Keep your pace natural.
- Interview: 45 seconds is short. Give your answer in the first sentence, then one reason and one example. If you finish early, add a second example or a short conclusion. Do not stop at 20 seconds.
> Interview timing: 0-5 s answer ("I'd say I prefer studying in the morning."), 5-25 s reason and example, 25-40 s extra detail or comparison, 40-45 s short closing sentence.
## Training your sense of time
- Practice with the timer on from the first week, even in section practice.
- Write your finishing time on each practice set. Watch the number go down.
- In full mocks, note where you lost time. Was it one academic passage? The Build a Sentence items? Fix that one place next week.
- Learn to let go. If one item has taken twice the average time, guess and move on. One item is never worth three.
## A note on stamina

There is no scheduled break, so your concentration must last the whole session. Late in the test, people read more slowly and make more careless errors. Full mocks in one sitting train this. See "Test anxiety and stamina".
